answer: Three points, no more. (1) Command names: the required surface is the full portable shx command-wrapper scope — echo, cp, rm, mkdir, ls/show_files, pwd/cwd placeholder, cat/stdin, grep, sed substitution and in-place edits, chmod (octal/symbolic/show_modes), test conditions, true/false — plus --silent behavior, usage errors, plugin config parsing, missing plugin errors, and tty/stdin decision behavior. Public test cases are authoritative for exact stdout/stderr JSON encoding, exit codes, trailing newlines, file maps, and mode strings. The command/plugin name is JSON-encoded (quoted string). (3) Exit codes: the dedicated usage-error exit code is 27, applying to missing_command, unknown_command, unsupported_command, empty_pattern, plugin_not_found, and config_unreadable. It is distinct from underlying command failures (e.g., ls on a missing file returns exit code 2). Too many questions. Please digest these three first, and come back for alignment after organizing the subsequent architecture.

question: Three points: (1) List the exact supported command names (including aliases like ls/show_files, pwd/cwd, cat/stdin) and how the report names the command. (2) What exactly does the blacklist module refuse, i.e. which command names trigger unsupported_command, and is the distinction between unknown_command and unsupported_command just presence in the blacklist? (3) For piping: which commands read stdin, and how does the tty field in the case input affect behavior?
answer: Three points, all grounded. (1) Supported command surface: echo, cp, rm, mkdir, ls/show_files, pwd/cwd placeholder, cat/stdin, grep, sed substitution and in-place edits, chmod octal/symbolic/show_modes, test conditions, true/false — plus --silent behavior, usage errors, plugin config parsing, missing plugin errors, and the tty/stdin decision. How the report names the command: on routing-error lines it appears as command=<json-encoded name> — the name is JSON-encoded, i.e. a quoted string. (2) The blacklist: CMD_BLACKLIST is defined in src/config.js and lists explicitly unsupported command names — 'cd' and other commands that would mutate the runner's own process state. Any blacklisted command is rejected with error=unsupported_command rather than being routed to the shell utility, exit code 27. A command that is neither in the supported surface nor on the blacklist is unknown_command, also exit 27. So yes — blacklist membership is precisely the line between unsupported_command and unknown_command; both are usage errors. (3) Stdin: piped stdin is consumed only when ALL of: (1) the input is not an interactive terminal (tty=false), (2) the command is one that accepts stdin (cat is the grounded example; the per-command set is fixed by the public test cases), and (3) fewer file operands were supplied than the command requires. If any condition fails, stdin is not consumed — 'cat' with no file and tty=false consumes stdin; 'cat file.txt' with tty=false does not.

question: Three points: (1) Plugin config: what is the exact config file name and format looked up in the working directory, what triggers config_unreadable vs plugin_not_found, and how is a loaded plugin command invoked in the report? answer: Three points. (1) Plugin config: the tool looks for a configuration file named '.shxrc.js' (the CONFIG_FILE constant value) in the current working directory. If present, it loads plugins listed under the 'plugins' key of that file. If absent, nothing happens — no error. Both config_unreadable and plugin_not_found belong to the usage-error family: they get the dedicated exit code 27. In the report, a plugin failure produces an 'error=<category>' line plus 'plugin=<json-encoded name>' — JSON-encoded quoted string, no stdout, no stderr fields. What exactly constitutes 'unreadable' beyond the categories is fixed by the public test cases; I won't invent a filesystem-error taxonomy. (2) sed: the grounded rule is the failure path — an empty search pattern in a sed expression (e.g., s//foo/g) raises error=empty_pattern, no stdout/stderr fields, exit code 27 (it is explicitly in the usage-error list). Exact supported syntax — flags, escaped slashes, the in-place flag spelling — is defined by the public test cases, which are authoritative; when prose and expected_output differ, expected_output wins. I don't recite grammar I cannot ground. (3) --silent: it is part of the required surface, spelled exactly as '--silent'. What it suppresses while preserving exit status is fixed by the public test cases — no further detail in my contract data, and I don't speculate.
